observations: All 5 parameterized mechanisms resolve EXECUTABLE with correct bound_action when correct parameters provided (C1 PASS)
All 5 parameterized mechanisms resolve UNKNOWN when parameters are missing (C2 PASS)
_bind() produces correct URL substitution for all 5 patterns including multi-slot (C3 PASS)
Parameterized mechanisms use MORE tokens than literal mechanisms for all 5 patterns, not fewer (C4 FAIL: 0/5)
Mean token savings is -6.4% (negative), far below the 15% threshold (C5 FAIL)
Token savings DECREASE with parameter count: 1-param mean -4.81%, 3-param -9.68% (C6 FAIL)
3-param pattern (pattern_5) has highest token penalty: -9.68% (3 extra tokens for 3 template slots)
Template variable names (id, userId, limit, page, category, minPrice, maxPrice) are longer than the concrete values they replace (1-3 char numbers)
Token cost of template syntax: ${varname} adds 3 chars overhead per slot ($ and { and }) plus varname length
Kernel regression tests pass 3/3 with no regression (C7 PASS)
validity_notes: Token measurement is tiktoken cl100k_base, not actual LLM inference tokenizer. Different tokenizers may produce different results.
Action_template JSON serialization includes both method and url fields. Token cost measured on JSON.dumps(sort_keys=True).
Training observations are hand-crafted synthetic data, not real browser sessions.
No network access, no browser automation, no model calls during measurement.
All mechanisms use confidence=0.9, above min_confidence threshold of 0.8.

The parent experiment reported 68 vs 96 tokens (29.17% savings) for a single pattern. That measurement may have used a different action_template structure or different URL representation. This experiment uses the same full-URL format for both literal and parameterized mechanisms, revealing that template syntax overhead exceeds concrete value savings for short numeric values.

Parameterized template savings require concrete values LONGER than the template variable name + syntax overhead (${varname} = varname.length + 3 chars). For short values (1-3 digit numbers), literal is more token-efficient.
The negative savings represent a real structural property: the ${var} template syntax adds fixed overhead per slot that dominates when replaced values are short.
unresolved: Whether parameterized representation saves tokens when concrete values are long strings (UUIDs, slugs, full paths) rather than short numeric IDs
